activities.anchor: Imagine a market where money has not been invented
activities.caption: call the size of the barter problem
activities.name: miBarterEst

config.prompt: With 1,000 different goods, barter needs a separate price for every pair. Roughly how many pairwise prices is that?
config.why: n(n−1)/2 = 1000 × 999 / 2 ≈ 500,000. Money replaces that whole matrix with one unit of account — the scale at which barter fails.
config.context: with 3 goods it is only 3 pairs; the count grows with the square

activities.anchor: Money is the technology that dissolves the problem
activities.caption: pair each job of money with its example
activities.name: miJobsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each job of money with what it makes possible:

pairs.right: the shoemaker accepts your money without wanting your chicken
every price is quoted in one yardstick, so thousands can be compared
savings keep their meaning between this month and next year

config.why: The three jobs are separate: exchange dissolves the double coincidence, the unit of account compresses the price list, and the store of value carries purchasing power through time.

activities.caption: which property does each candidate fail?
activities.name: miPropertySort

config.prompt: Which property of good money does each candidate fail?

items.label: pebbles on a beach — anyone can gather more
unlimited sand — supply is effectively infinite
fresh fish — spoils by the next day
ice sculptures — melt in the market
a grand piano — not exactly pocket-sized

config.why: Money must be scarce, durable, portable and divisible; each candidate fails one test. A painting can be scarce and durable yet still fail divisibility.

activities.caption: how a bank loan creates money
activities.name: miLoanOrder

config.prompt: How a bank loan creates money — put the steps in order:
items: A bank approves your mortgage and credits your account
The deposit is new money — no saver's pounds were moved
You spend it, and the seller's bank receives the deposit
You repay the loan over the years
As the loan is repaid, that money is destroyed
config.why: Most money is bank-created credit: loans create deposits, and repayment extinguishes them.

activities.anchor: Economists measure the result in two headlines
activities.caption: fill the blanks — M1 and M2
activities.name: miMoneyCloze

config.text: M1 is currency plus %%0%% deposits — money you can spend immediately. M2 adds %%1%% accounts and certificates of deposit. Most money is created by bank %%2%%, not by printing notes.
config.hint: M1 is the spend-now measure; M2 widens it to less liquid savings.

activities.anchor: The distinction that organises everything else
activities.caption: find the real-versus-nominal slip
activities.name: miRealSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the real-versus-nominal reasoning goes wrong:
lines: Your pay rises 5% while prices rise 7%.
Nominal pay is up, so your real pay has risen too.
Your real pay has fallen by about 2%.
Borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain in this situation.
config.correction: Nominal pay rose, but real pay fell: 5% − 7% ≈ −2%.
config.why: Inflation redistributes from savers to borrowers: borrowers repay in cheaper money, while fixed-income savers lose.

activities.anchor: converts any growth rate into a halving
activities.caption: mark the doubling time at 5%
activities.name: miRulePlace

config.prompt: At 5% inflation, roughly how many years until prices double? Place it on the axis.
config.why: 70 ÷ 5 = 14 years. At 3% it is about 23 years; at 10%, 7 years.

activities.anchor: is too much spending chasing too few goods
activities.caption: diagnose the oil shock
activities.name: miOilBranch

config.root: Crude oil roughly quadruples in a few months. Trace the diagnosis.

start.text: Energy feeds into almost everything. Which inflation does this shock start?

choices.label: Cost-push — input prices rise and firms pass them on
choices.feedback: Yes — an input shock raises costs across the economy.

choices.label: Demand-pull — too much spending chasing too few goods
choices.feedback: Spending did not surge; the cost of an essential input did.

choices.label: Deflation — prices are falling
choices.feedback: This shock pushes prices up, not down.

cost.text: Cost-push. The central bank now faces a dilemma: higher rates cool demand but cannot produce more oil. What is the main risk?

choices.label: A wage–price spiral if expectations unanchor
choices.feedback: Yes — expected inflation can make the shock persistent.

choices.label: Inflation vanishes immediately
choices.feedback: Cost shocks fade slowly, and expectations can keep them alive.

spiral.text: If workers and firms expect 10% and set wages and prices at 10%, a temporary shock becomes persistent. Credibility is the shield.

demand.text: That is the wrong diagnosis: spending did not surge; the cost of an essential input did. Raising demand further would worsen it.

defl.text: Deflation is falling prices — the opposite of an oil shock.

choices.label: Reconsider the diagnosis
choices.feedback: Which way does a cost shock push prices?

instant.text: Cost shocks fade slowly, and expectations can keep them alive.

choices.label: Follow the risk
choices.feedback: Track what happens if expectations unanchor.

config.why: An oil shock is cost-push; the policy danger is that a one-off price jump becomes a wage–price spiral once expectations unanchor.

activities.anchor: is the central bank steering demand
activities.caption: true or false — the monetary lever
activities.name: miPolicyJudge

statements.s: A central bank raises its interest rate; mortgage and investment spending cool, and inflation pressure eases after a lag.
statements.why: Higher rates raise borrowing costs, which cools demand — but the transmission runs through decisions that take months to renegotiate.

statements.s: The main effect on inflation appears within days of a rate change.
statements.why: The standard lag is a year or more, which is why central banks must forecast rather than react to the latest headline.

statements.s: Central bank independence helps because governments may be tempted to stimulate before elections.
statements.why: The political business cycle is the temptation; independence protects credibility.

activities.caption: hyperinflation versus deflation — drag the divider
activities.name: miDiseaseCompare

config.prompt: Two failures of price stability — drag the divider:

before.label: hyperinflation
before.text: prices double every few days; money stops being a store of value, and people flee to barter or foreign currency

after.label: deflation
after.text: prices fall, so buyers wait; debts grow heavier in real terms and spending stalls

config.why: Both are failures of price stability in opposite directions; the 2% target is a buffer against deflation, which is harder to escape.
